summary.text:
A short, clean two-page appendix that documents one strategic decision. Against an original 2025/26 estimate of £70.000m internal borrowing at year end, East Sussex closed the year £112.919m under-borrowed — £42.919m further internal than planned. The appendix explains it plainly on page 2: no new long-term external borrowing was undertaken during 2025/26 in support of the strategic decision to delay borrowing whilst interest rates remain elevated.

The cash side of the same decision is visible in the investments table on page 1. Average investment balances fell from £151.972m in Q1 to £51.074m in Q4, and cash investments at 31 March came in at £30.4m, down 74% from £115.3m a year earlier. Investment returns beat SONIA in all four quarters, by 31–46 basis points.

The loan book reconciles exactly. All 47 PWLB loans in our file total £200,141,602 at a weighted 4.3781%, against the paper's £200.142m at 4.38% on page 1 — to the pound and to the basis point. 60% of the book sits over ten years and the biggest discounts on that tail are 2046–2056 positions at 4.10–4.15% coupons; on the DMO's premature repayment curve today the indicative discount across the 46 loans now live is about £21m on £198m of principal (roughly 10.7%), which is a mark-to-market observation from the other side of the elevated-rates environment that shaped the year's decision. Neither the maturity profile nor the borrowing limits show any breach.

officer.subject: Your 2025/26 outturn was £42.9m more under-borrowed than planned
officer.body:
Hi [name],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts drawn from your Appendix 2 to the 30 June Cabinet — the Q4 2025/26 treasury indicators. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The two-page format actually makes the year's decision easier to read than most.

A cross-check first, so you can see our figures tie to yours. We hold all 47 of your PWLB loans and price them daily — £200,141,602 at a weighted 4.3781% — which is your borrowing table on page 1 exactly, to the pound and to the basis point. That's at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis if useful.

The thing worth flagging is what the year's decision looks like when the two indicators sit next to each other. Your original 2025/26 strategy planned for £70.000m of under-borrowing at year end; the outturn was £112.919m — £42.919m further internal than planned. Alongside that, average investment balances went from £151.972m in Q1 to £51.074m in Q4, and cash investments at 31 March came in at £30.4m, down 74% from £115.3m a year earlier. The appendix explains it plainly on page 2: no new long-term external borrowing during 2025/26, in support of the strategic decision to delay whilst rates remain elevated. It's a stated bet, and the cash line is where its cost sits so far.

On the other side of the same decision, your existing book helps. 60% of the borrowing sits over ten years, and the biggest discounts on that tail are on positions maturing 2046-2056 at 4.10-4.15% coupons; on the DMO's premature repayment curve today (notice 314/26 PM, 14 August) our indicative discount across the 46 loans now live — one £2m matured after year-end — is about £21m against £198m of balances, or roughly 10.7%. That's mark-to-market on our engine only, not a quote (only the DMO's is binding), and it models no MRP or accounting treatment. Per-loan breakdown is on the same loan-analysis page.

The wider market view is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, where the monthly sector data is worth a look when the 2026/27 external borrowing question comes back into view — July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers, average 5.02%, after the thinnest May in years, which gives a read on whether the market is thinning or opening up before any roll or new draw.

None of it needs a meeting or a subscription, and the rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds to check. On training, four fit where East Sussex is: Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the decision on when to take on external debt; Liquidity and cashflow forecasting, for the cash headroom sitting alongside it; The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR), for the £42.9m gap between planned and outturn under-borrowing; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
